title: The Responsibility Gap: AI and the Shift to True Security Accountability

segments.text: >> ANNOUNCER: Please welcome co‑Chief Executive Officer
Tenable, Stephen Vintz.
>> STEPHEN VINTZ: Good afternoon!
You've heard a lot about AI this week and guess what?
You're about to hear more, but from a different perspective.
The AI story really begins in 1956 when researchers from a
Dartmouth Workshop confidently predicted that machines would
soon think like humans.
Seventy years later they now produce amazing things
like essays, artwork, and extremely confident, and often
very wrong answers.
So should you be worried about AI?
I'll get back to you on that.
As the co‑CEO of Tenable, I lead a company that has access
to vast amounts of exposure data.
This data tells us all kinds of interesting stories.
So today I'm going to share a few stories
with you -- actually, three seemingly plausible stories,
stories of how AI can go wrong.
Your job is to guess which one's true.
Ready?
Okay, story number one.
Recently, a major financial institution
rolled out an internal AI Assistant powered by OpenAI.
It was meant to help employees work faster,
summarize documents, and analyze data.
And people loved it.
Usage exploded across the company.
But there was a problem no one noticed.
The Agent unknowingly had access to confidential
information such as financial models, strategic documents,
internal communications, the kinds of things you
absolutely do not want broadly exposed.
As a result, employees, thousands of them could query
it and pull information out of it that others were
not meant to see.
And the exposure?
Well, it wasn't caused by a hacker.
It was a simple misconfiguration.
And who set it up?
The security team.
The very group responsible for protecting the organization.
And now for our second story.
A company began piloting an AI‑powered enterprise
search platform to eliminate data silos.
Now, the goal was to provide a unified view
across the organization of all customer interactions.
That sounds pretty good actually.
Now, during the POV, the company tried to jailbreak the
technology and was successful.
The result?
The AI started to hallucinate and speculate where the CISO
was spending his time.
It actually theorized that he was working on a secret
acquisition and plotting against others in the company.
What started as a contained experiment, threatened to become
a reputational crisis.
And now our third story.
A sales rep at a vendor software company used an
authorized AI Age3nt to analyze conversations with prospects
for use in follow-up calls.
One of the major outcomes of the Agent was to identify all
key stakeholders at the prospect and to
provide the vendor with personalized insights on each.
Now, the good news is, the report created by the Agent
assigned a very high probability of close
for the deal.
The bad news is, the report contained inflammatory
language and heavily criticized certain individuals
at the prospect company.
Now, to make matters worse, the report was mistakenly emailed
to the executive sponsor at the prospect by the sales rep.
And needless to say, they lost the deal.
So, which one of these stories is true?
If you guessed all of them, which many
of you did, you're right!
Tenable has observed these incidents directly.
Embarrassing and problematic?
Yes, but not catastrophic, except for maybe that rep
who emailed the report.
So, should you be worried about AI?
Again, I'll get back to you on that.
But here's what's really concerning.
As hospitals begin deploying AI in the
operating room for enhanced surgical precision,
reports arise of botched surgeries, misidentified
body parts, strokes, and other severe outcomes.
AI‑enabled weapons systems already exist today.
The UN has warned that autonomous systems
may struggle to uphold humanitarian law.
They may even escalate conflicts faster than
humans can respond.
And sadly, very sadly, in British Columbia,
the family of a 12‑year old mass shooting victim has filed a
lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging that the company failed
to alert authorities.
That GPT prompted by the shooter
signaled impending violence.
Now, these aren't hypothetical-use cases.
They're real‑world examples of AI's use today,
and they're becoming more perilous and more pervasive.
If left unchecked, AI could create a
medical crisis, could destabilize military operations
and even threaten public safety.
So now, now should you be worried about AI?
Maybe.
But surely, someone is accountable and owns
AI risk, right?
Is it the user who wanted the app?
Is it the IT team who provisioned it?
Is it the security team or the CISO who is supposed to vet it
or even the CFO or the CEO?
At this point, patients, civilians, and investors
they're beginning to bear the risks and costs
of AI downstream.
Certainly, they shouldn't be responsible.
Maybe everyone's responsible.
So maybe you should be worried because
if everyone's responsible, then no one's responsible!
And this is the responsibility gap, and we must close it.
One of the key challenges is that AI
systems are meaningfully more complex to deploy than
traditional SaaS apps, not just technically,
but also organizationally.
You see, the data science team owns the models.
The ML ops team owns the production pipeline.
IT owns the deployment.
Product team owns the integration of
these capabilities into the offering.
Legal owns the compliance.
And what about security team, by the way?
Well, the security team is left at the end of the line
trying to protect a system they didn't design
and don't fully control.
The responsibility gap exists, in part because AI ownership is
fractured, very fractured within the enterprise.
And here's the reality.
When something goes wrong, when data is leaked, when a
model is poisoned, and when a brand is tarnished, and when
there are significant costs and damages, it's the CEO and
the Board who are held liable.
Now, for some this may feel like a déjà vu moment
because we've seen this pattern before.
Every decade or so, a major technology shift emerges that
makes us reconsider everything we know about security and risk.
Think about that.
The PC era gave way to endpoint security
and host‑based firewalls.
The Internet necessitated network security and
vulnerability management and the shift to cloud gave us all
kinds of crazy acronyms in security like CNAPP,
and CSPM, and CWP, and DSPM.
And while AI is that next market‑defining shift,
its velocity, its ubiquity, and its autonomy is like
anything we've seen before.
Consider Google's Gemini.
Google's Gemini has over 750 million monthly users.
ChatGPT, has over 800 million, and that number is expected to
triple this year.
You see, the latency between innovation and mass adoption
has effectively vanished.
There is a fundamental mismatch between the
exponential speed of AI adoption and the linear
speed of traditional corporate governance.
And things will only move faster and only
become more complex.
Roughly 90 percent of all organizations have adopted
AI in some form.
And yet half of those have already experienced some
sort of cyber incident.
That's a staggering number for a technology that's still
in its infancy.
Now, speed aside, because AI has become ubiquitous,
it's quickly democratized application development.
In a short span of time, an avalanche of no‑code AI
platforms have emerged that enable everyone and anyone to
develop Agents with little or no coding experience.
These "citizen developers" are everywhere, vibe coding
without regard for security.
And that's when humans are involved at all.
As we delegate more work to AI Agents, we're also entering a
crisis of autonomy.
Today, AI Agents have access to vast amounts of data,
can write code, can trigger workflows without
prior approval and without humans in the loop.
And unlike humans, AI Agents lack a moral compass
and operate without regard for whether the actions they
take are appropriate.
And many of these Agents go on to form multi‑Agent networks
where they communicate directly with one another.
As multi-Agent proliferate and become more interconnected,
the attack surface expands and the chances of
a self‑induced crisis becomes more likely.
So given all of this, what do we do?
Well, to close the Responsibility Gap,
we have to get serious about how we manage this technology.
And effective risk management and governance needs to happen
in both the public sector and the private sector.
Let's start with the public sector.
Regulators play a massive role in setting the tone and tempo
for safety and their focus should be twofold.
First, they should focus on AI outcomes, not the tech itself
and how it's built, because specific technical
architectures can quickly become obsolete in the AI era.
Effective outcome‑based approaches reduce the risk
related to bias, such as training and algorithmic bias,
reduce the risk related to misuse, and reduce the risk
related to targeted attacks like prompt injection.
These are unintended consequences of
uncontrolled AI deployments.
Now, last Friday, March 20th, the White House released a
legislative framework to promote AI innovation and to
create a single, nationwide law that
preempts state regulations.
It prioritizes child safety, energy use,
IP and workforce development.
We also need a framework for security, which brings me to
my second area of focus for regulators.
Now, I know the tech sector does not like to be regulated,
but here's the good news.
While the velocity, the ubiquity, and
the autonomy, they're fundamentally different with AI.
The security frameworks we use to regulate it don't have to be.
The NIST Cybersecurity framework, for example,
in the U.S. is a great place to start.
And it's widely recognized as the standard
for managing cyber risk.
It's flexible enough to be adapted for AI‑enabled threats,
via AI profiles, without creating a compliance nightmare.
And at the international level, because that is really
important too, ISO cybersecurity standards,
they're already in use by some countries,
where appropriate modifications have been made to bridge the gap
between general security and AI security.
You see the mix of discovering assets and systems,
identifying critical exposures, and monitoring
for drift, applies as naturally to an AI Agent as
a traditional server.
Also, OWASP's GenAI Security Project provides the practical
tools to secure Agentic AI without slowing innovation.
And that's important.
So, regulators set the rules of the road.
But the responsibility of governance ultimately resides
with the private sector.
And there the responsibility is also twofold.
First, we need to think about risk proactively.
For over 30 years, our industry has been built
on firefighting detecting breaches and responding
at human speed.
That made sense when attacks moved at human speed.
It was the right way to operate.
But it fails in the AI era where everything moves
at machine speed.
And our spending, our spending reflects this outdated reality.
Today, over 90 percent of all cybersecurity spend is in
detection of response, while, disproportionally,
a much smaller percentage is in prevention
and proactive risk reduction.
We're spending over 90 cents of every dollar firefighting,
waiting for plumes of smoke to appear, when instead
we should be fireproofing.
This is where exposure management comes in,
which is all about unified visibility, insight and action,
not only to understand risk, but to
reduce it proactively and holistically because risk rarely
appears in isolation.
An overprivileged identity here, a misconfigured workload
there, or a crucial vulnerability in
a model somewhere else individually may look harmless.
But chained together, they can create a lethal attack path.
Exposure management also provides the necessary
intelligence layer to orchestrate the right mix
of humans and AI to get stuff done because
that's really important.
This means providing context, providing direction,
and providing the validation to actively reduce risk.
Now, this matters, because often AI makes probabilistic
recommendations based on observed patterns, whereas
security, true security, must operate on deterministic facts.
It's the clarity that's key here.
And when you have clarity about where your risk resides,
you can act with confidence, and confidence
is what ultimately drives accountability.
Now, the second responsibility for the private sector is to
ensure that risk management is embedded to every single layer
in the organization because AI adoption isn't
is so widespread.
Risk assessment can't be done in silos.
The developer, the data scientist, the business leader
all need to be evaluating risk through the same lens.
That starts with identifying risks prior to deployment and
understanding the blast radius if a model goes sideways.
Also, an AI governance committee should be established
consisting of cross-functional leadership to ensure risks are
continuously monitored in accordance with the
company's risk profile and regulatory framework.
But while the responsibility is distributed,
accountability is not.
And ultimately, the company is responsible for
the machine's actions, and there's even legal precedent
to this effect.
And if neither the private sector nor the AI
model companies are able to effectively manage this
profound risk, governments may conclude that AI should
be treated like other critical technologies such as
aerospace and cryptography.
This means we could see AI become nationalized or at the
very least heavily regulated beyond anything
we've ever seen before in the tech industry.
Okay.
So let's bring this back to you because closing the
responsibility gap doesn't happen through technology alone.
It happens through accountability.
We're entering a world where the same people responsible for
cloud risk, infra risk, identity risk will also
be responsible for deploying AI and having AI run
inside their environments.
And risk cannot live in a separate silo,
which means the people in this room today have a new
role to play.
If you're a CISO or a security practitioner, you need to think
about risk holistically, not just through the lens
of your team, but across the organization because
that's how AI is deployed.
And let's face it, AI does not care about your org charts.
Risk isn't a spectator sport.
You, you're the manifestation of governance.
And if you're advising a board or sitting on one,
AI risk must become a standing conversation.
Boards will increasingly expect visibility into how
AI is deployed, what risks it introduces, and how those
risks are being managed because in the AI era,
visibility is accountability.
We must choose visibility over blindness.
We must choose fireproofing over firefighting because
without accountability, velocity becomes volatility.
And that, that is the responsibility gap, but with
accountability, AI becomes something very different --
not a source of chaos, but a capability we can trust,
not an accelerator of exposure, but an
accelerator of resilience.
The future of AI will be shaped by the choices
we make today.
And in a world, a world, where every company is an
AI company, trust, trust will be the only
currency that survives.
Thank you.
